heading_path.h3: Units of measurement for area

record.evidence_quote: We measure the area of a two-dimensional shape by counting or working out how many unit squares will fit into the space. Examples of units of measurement for area are $\text{mm}^{2}$, $\text{cm}^{2}$, $\text{m}^{2}$, or even $\text{km}^{2}$. - A square millimetre ($\text{mm}^{2}$) is a tiny square with sides each one m
record.content_text:
We measure the area of a two-dimensional shape by counting or working out how many unit squares will fit into the space. Examples of units of measurement for area are $\text{mm}^{2}$, $\text{cm}^{2}$, $\text{m}^{2}$, or even $\text{km}^{2}$.

- A square millimetre ($\text{mm}^{2}$) is a tiny square with sides each one millimetre long. It is about the size of a flattened breadcrumb.
- A square centimetre ($\text{cm}^{2}$) is the size of a square with sides that are one centimetre long. It is about the size of your thumbnail.
- A square metre ($\text{m}^{2}$) is the size of a square with sides each one metre long. It is about the space on the floor that you need to sit cross-legged.
- A square kilometre ($\text{km}^{2}$) is the space inside a square with sides that are one kilometre long. It is a very big unit for measuring area. You can fit about ten football fields into one square kilometre.

record_links.rationale: This record explains finding area by counting grid squares.

heading_path.h3: Determine area by counting squares on grid

record.evidence_quote: If a diagram is drawn on a grid, you can simply count the squares to find the area of the shape. Each small square on the grid can represent a square in real life. - One small square on the grid can represent an area of 1 m by 1 m: $$ \text {1 m} \times \text{1 m} = \text{1 $\text m^{2}$} $$ - One small square on the g
record.content_text:
If a diagram is drawn on a grid, you can simply count the squares to find the area of the shape. Each small square on the grid can represent a square in real life.

- One small square on the grid can represent an area of 1 m by 1 m:

$$
\text {1 m} \times \text{1 m} = \text{1 $\text m^{2}$}
$$

- One small square on the grid can represent an area of 1 cm by 1 cm:

$$
\text{1 cm} \times \text{1 cm} = \text{1 cm}^{2}
$$

heading_path.h3: Using formulae to calculate area

record.evidence_quote: If a shape is not drawn on a grid, you cannot find the area of the shape by counting the squares, but there are formulae that you can use to calculate area. You can check that the formulae are correct by comparing the answers when you use the two different methods. The method of counting the squares should give you the
record.content_text:
If a shape is not drawn on a grid, you cannot find the area of the shape by counting the squares, but there are formulae that you can use to calculate area.

You can check that the formulae are correct by comparing the answers when you use the two different methods. The method of counting the squares should give you the same answer as when you use a formula to calculate the area of a shape.

In the two worked examples below, you will first count the squares and then use a formula to find the area. In each case you will see that the two answers are the same.

record_links.rationale: This worked example derives and uses the area formula for a rectangle.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 12.14: Comparing methods of calculating area of a rectangle

record.evidence_quote: Source math retained: \times ^{2} ^{2} \times \begin{array}{ll} \text{Area of rectangle} & {= \text{length} \times \text{breadth}}\\ &{= l \times b} \\ &{= \text{9 km} \times \text{4 km}} \\ &{= \text{36}\ {\text{km}^{2}}} \end{array} ^{2}
record.prompt_text: Find the area of the rectangle provided by counting squares. Each square on the grid represents a square of 1 km by 1 km. Then work out a formula for calculating the area of a rectangle, and check the answer you get by comparing it to your first answer.
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Remember that area is the amount of flat space taken up by a shape. Count the number of squares on the grid that are covered by the rectangle.

The rectangle consists of 9 columns of smaller squares. Each column has 4 smaller squares. So there are 9 $\times$ 4 = 36 squares inside the rectangle.

Area of rectangle = 36 km$^{2}$

Step 2: Use your calculation above to work out a formula to calculate the area of a rectangle.

You can see that 9 km is the length of the rectangle, and 4 km is the breadth. To get the area, you multiplied 9 by 4, so what you did was multiply the length by the breadth. Then you wrote in the square units, which this time is km$^{2}$.

So the formula for the area of a rectangle is length $\times$ breadth.

Step 3: Use the formula to calculate the area.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Area of rectangle} &{= \text{length} \times \text{breadth}}\\
&{= l \times b} \\
&{= \text{9 km} \times \text{4 km}} \\
&{= \text{36}\ {\text{km}^{2}}}
\end{array}
$$

Step 4: Compare this answer with your first answer.

Both methods give the same answer: A = 36 km$^{2}$.

record_links.rationale: This worked example derives and uses the area formula for a square.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 12.15: Comparing methods of calculating area of a square

record.evidence_quote: Source math retained: \times ^{2} ^{2} \times \begin{array}{ll} \text{Area of square} & { = \text{side} \times \text{side}}\\ &{= \text{9 cm} \times \text{9 cm}} \\ &{= \text{81}\ {\text{cm}^{2}}} \end{array} ^{2}
record.prompt_text: Find the area of the square provided by counting squares. Each square on the grid represents a square of 1 cm by 1 cm. Then work out a formula for calculating the area of a square, and check the answer you get by comparing it to your first answer.
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Count the number of squares on the grid that are covered by the square.

The square consists of 9 rows of squares and 9 columns of squares. So there are 9 $\times$ 9 = 81 squares inside the square.

Area of square = 81 cm$^{2}$

Step 2: Use your calculation to work out a formula to calculate the area of a square.

In a square, all four sides are the same length. To get the area, you multiplied 9 by 9, so what you did was multiply the length by the length (or we can say the side by the side). So the area is just the product of the two (equal) sides. Then you wrote in the square units, which this time is cm$^{2}$.

So the formula for the area of a square is side $\times$ side.

Step 3: Use the formula to calculate the area.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Area of square} & { = \text{side} \times \text{side}}\\
&{= \text{9 cm} \times \text{9 cm}} \\
&{= \text{81}\ {\text{cm}^{2}}}
\end{array}
$$

Step 4: Compare this answer with your first answer.

Both methods give the same answer: A = 81 cm$^{2}$.

heading_path.h3: Formulae for the area of a two-dimensional shape

record.evidence_quote: It will help you if you memorise the formulae for area, so that you can use them easily when you need to. Understanding where the formulae come from will help you to memorise them. - **Rectangle:** Area of a rectangle = length $\times$ breadth. - **Square:** Area of a square $= s \times s = s^{2}$ - **Triangle:** Area
record.content_text:
It will help you if you memorise the formulae for area, so that you can use them easily when you need to. Understanding where the formulae come from will help you to memorise them.

- **Rectangle:** Area of a rectangle = length $\times$ breadth.
- **Square:** Area of a square $= s \times s = s^{2}$
- **Triangle:** Area of a triangle $= \frac{b \times h}{2}$.
- **Parallelogram:** Area of a parallelogram $= b \times h$.
- **Trapezium:** Area of a trapezium $= \frac{h}{2}\left( a + b \right)$.
- **Circle:** Area of a circle $= \pi \times r^{2}$.

With a triangle, the base ($b$) and the height ($h$) must be perpendicular to each other, or you will not get the correct answer.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 12.19: Finding area of a parallelogram using a formula

record.evidence_quote: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 20 cm and height 14 cm.
record.prompt_text: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 20 cm and height 14 cm.
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Write down the correct formula for the area of a parallelogram.

$$
A  = b \times h
$$

Step 2: Substitute the correct values into the formula.

$$
\begin{align}
 A & = b \times h\\
 &= 20  \times 14
\end{align}
$$

Step 3: Do the calculation and remember to show the correct units in your answer.

$$
\begin{align}
 A & = b \times h \\
 &= 20 \times 14 \\
 &= \text{280}\text{ cm$^{2}$}
\end{align}
$$

heading_path.h3: Worked example 12.20: Finding area of a trapezium using a formula

record.evidence_quote: Find the area of a trapezium with height 6 cm and parallel sides 7 cm and 15 cm.
record.prompt_text: Find the area of a trapezium with height 6 cm and parallel sides 7 cm and 15 cm.
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Write down the correct formula for the area of a trapezium.

$$
A = \frac{h}{2}\left( a + b \right)
$$

Step 2: Substitute the correct values into the formula.

$$
\begin{align}
 A &= \frac{h}{2}\left( a + b \right)\\
 &= \frac{6 }{2}\left( 7  + 15  \right)
\end{align}
$$

Step 3: Do the calculation and remember to show the correct units in your answer.

$$
\begin{align}
 A &= \frac{h}{2}\left( a + b \right)\\
 & = \frac{6 }{2}\left(7  + 15  \right)\\
 &= 3 \times 22  \\
 & = \text{66}\text{ cm$^{2}$}
\end{align}
$$

record.prompt_text:
### Exercise 12.10: Use formulae to calculate area

12. The circle has a diameter of 6 km. What is its area? Use 3.14 for $\pi$.
record.answer_text:
The diameter of a circle is always double the radius, so $d = 2r$. So if the diameter is 6 km, the radius is 3 km.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
A & {= \pi \times r^{2}} \\
& {= 3.14 \times 3^{2}} \\
& {= 3.14 \times 9} \\
& {= \text{50.24} {\text{ km}^{2}}} \\
\end{array}
$$

record.content_text:
Sometimes we have to calculate the area of an irregular shape. Remember that in an irregular polygon, all the sides are not the same length and all the angles are not equal.

Often the irregular shape you are given to work with will be made up of two or more regular shapes. To calculate the area, you divide the irregular shape into simpler shapes, usually squares or rectangles, that have familiar area formulae.

record_links.rationale: This worked example calculates the area of an irregular plane shape by decomposing it into rectangles and squares.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 12.22: Finding area of irregular shape by counting squares

record.evidence_quote: Determine the area of the given shape. Each square represents a $\text{1}\ \text{cm} \times \text{1}\ \text{cm}$ area.
record.prompt_text: Determine the area of the given shape. Each square represents a $\text{1}\ \text{cm} \times \text{1}\ \text{cm}$ area.
record.answer_text:
Step 1: See what shapes you can break the shape into.

The shape can be divided into the yellow rectangle $Y$, and the blue square $Z$.

Step 2: Calculate the area of the rectangle, $Y$. Use the formula for the area of a rectangle.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
 \text{Area}_{Y} & {= \text{length} \times \text{breadth}} \\
 & {= 8 \times 3} \\
 & {= \text{24}\ {\text{cm}^{2}}} \\
 \end{array}
$$

Step 3: Calculate the area of the square, $Z$. Use the formula for the area of a square.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
 \text{Area}_{Z} & {= \text{side} \times \text{side}} \\
 & {= 2 \times 2} \\
 & {= \text{4}\ {\text{cm}^{2}}} \\
 \end{array}
$$

Step 4: Add the area of the square and the area of the rectangle together to get the total area of the shape. Remember to show the correct units in your answer.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
 \text{Area}_\text{Total} & {= \text{Area}_{Y} + \text{Area}_{Z}} \\
 & {= \text{28}\ {\text{cm}^{2}}} \\
 \end{array}
$$

Therefore, the area of the shape is $\text{28}\ {\text{cm}^{2}}$.

record_links.rationale: This worked example calculates the area of an irregular plane shape by decomposing it into a square and rectangle.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 12.23: Finding area of irregular shape by counting squares

record.evidence_quote: Calculate the area of the shape below, using the given lengths in cm.
record.prompt_text: Calculate the area of the shape below, using the given lengths in cm.
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Break the shape into familiar, regular polygons.

The shape can be divided into a rectangle, labelled $B$, and a square, labelled $A$.

Step 2: Find the area of the square labelled $A$.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
 \text{Area}_{A} & {= \text{side} \times \text{side}} \\
 & {= 4 \times 4} \\
 & {= \text{16 cm}^{2}} \\
 \end{array}
$$

Step 3: Find the area of the rectangle labelled $B$.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
 \text{Area}_{B} & {= \text{length} \times \text{breadth}} \\
  & {= 8 \times 3} \\
  & {= \text{24 cm}^{2}} \\
 \end{array}
$$

Step 4: Find the sum of the two areas.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
 \text{Area}_\text{Total} & {= \text{Area}_{A} + \text{Area}_{B}}\\
 & {= \text{16 cm}^{2} + \text{24 cm}{2}}\\
 & {= \text{40 cm}^{2}}
 \end{array}
$$

record.prompt_text:
### Exercise 12.11: Calculate the area of irregular shapes

3. In the diagram below, one of the lengths of the sides has been replaced by $z$. The other five sides have the lengths shown in the figure. All of the angles in the shape are right angles, as labelled.

Determine the value of $z$. Then find the area for this figure. All lengths in the figure have dimensions in mm.
record.answer_text:
Start by finding $z$. The sides opposite each other are parallel to each other, because all the angles are right angles. So you can use the sides parallel to $z$, which are 3 mm and 5 mm long.

The side labelled $z$ has the same length as the two opposite sides added together. So we can write this equation to find $z$:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
z & {= 5 + 3} \\
& {= 8} \\
\end{array}
$$

The length of $z$ is 8 mm.

Now we can break the shape into two rectangles to find the area.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Area}_{A} & {= l \times b} \\
 & {= 9 \times 3} \\
 & {= \text{27 mm}^{2}} \\
\text{Area}_{B} & {= l \times b} \\
 & {= 3 \times 5} \\
 & {= \text{15 mm}^{2}} \\
\text{Area}_\text{Total} & {= \text{Area}_{A} + \text{Area}_{B}} \\
 & {= \text{42 mm}^{2}} \\
\end{array}
$$

record_links.rationale: This item asks learners to determine a missing length and calculate area.

### Exercise 12.11: Calculate the area of irregular shapes

4. In the shape below, one of the lengths of the sides has been replaced by $z$. The other five sides have the lengths shown. All of the angles are right angles, as labelled.

Determine the value of $z$. Then find the area of this shape. All lengths are in mm.
record.answer_text:
Start by finding $z$. All the angles are right angles, so you can use the sides parallel to $z$, which are 4 mm and 5 mm long.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
z & {= 4 + 5} \\
& {= 9}
\end{array}
$$

Now we break the shape into two rectangles to find the area.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Area}_{A} & {= l \times b} \\
 & {= 9 \times 5} \\
 & {= \text{45 mm}^{2}} \\
\text{Area}_{B} & {= l \times b} \\
 & {= 4 \times 4} \\
 & {= \text{16 mm}^{2}} \\
\text{Area}_\text{Total} & {= \text{Area}_{A} + \text{Area}_{B}} \\
 & {= \text{61 mm}^{2}} \\
\end{array}
$$
